documentation.range:
The Common Dolphin is a widely distributed oceanic species that occurs from tropical to cool temperate waters of the Atlantic, Pacific, and Indian Oceans (Perrin 2018). Within the Atlantic Ocean, it appears to be absent from the Gulf of Mexico and from of the Caribbean Sea (except for the region around Venezuela, where a coastal population occurs; Jefferson et al. 2009). It occurs in a range of habitat types, including nearshore waters as well as open-sea waters thousands of kilometres offshore. Common Dolphins regularly occur in some enclosed seas, such as the Okhotsk Sea and Sea of Japan, and separate subpopulations exist in the Mediterranean Sea and a subspecies in the Black Sea. Once one of the most common cetaceans in the Mediterranean Sea, the Common Dolphins there have undergone a generalized and major reduction in geographic range since the 1970s (Bearzi et al. 2003). Common Dolphins occur as far south as southeastern South Africa and Namibia in Africa; southern Australia and New Zealand; and Argentina and northern Chile (Finday et al. 1992, Durante et al. 2016). In the Northern Hemisphere they extend to the UK, Norway, Korea, Japan and Canada (Caputo et al. 2017, Song et al. 2014, Jefferson et al. 2015). Common Dolphins occur regularly in the Persian Gulf (Braulik et al. 2010, Preen 2004) and in the Red Sea (Notarbartolo di Sciara et al. 2017).

Distributions of the four currently recognized subspecies of Common Dolphins are as follows:

  • Delphinus delphis delphis: the nominate subspecies occurs throughout the entire range of the species, except the Black Sea and Indian Ocean.
  • Delphinus delphis bairdii: this subspecies appears to be found in distinct areas and apparently-disjunct subpopulations are known from central California to southern Mexico, and possibly Peru. Dolphins assigned to this subspecies generally occur within about 180 km of the coast.
  • Delphinus delphis tropicalis: this subspecies occurs in the Indo-Pacific from at least the Red Sea/Somalia to western Taiwan, southern China, Indonesia, the Gulf of Thailand and the Persian Gulf (Jefferson and Van Waerebeek 2002).
  • Delphinus delphis ponticus: This small-bodied subspecies is found only in the Black Sea and adjacent waters (Birkun 2008).
documentation.population:
This is a widespread species and the available abundance estimates are primarily from the Northern Hemisphere. There are very few abundance estimates from the Southern Hemisphere, which constitutes a large portion of the species range. Studies of Common Dolphin abundance in each ocean basin or sea are summarized (but not exhaustively) below.

Pacific Ocean
The abundance of Common Dolphins in the eastern Tropical Pacific (ETP) was estimated from eight vessel-based line-transect surveys conducted between 1986 and 2000 as 2,963,000 (CV=24%) (Gerrodette and Forcada 2002). In 2006, Common Dolphins were again judged to be the most abundant cetaceans in the ETP and were estimated at 3,127,203 (CV=26%) individuals (Gerrodette et al. 2008). The most recent estimate of abundance off California, Oregon and Washington, determined from the geometric mean of estimates from 2008 and 2014 summer/autumn vessel-based line transect surveys was 969,861 (CV = 0.17) Short-beaked Common Dolphins, and 101,305 (CV=0.49) Eastern North Pacific Long-beaked Common Dolphins (Barlow 2016). These estimates include correction factors for animals missed during the surveys (Barlow 2016).

There are an estimated 1.4 million Common Dolphins in the Western Pacific off Japan (Kanaji et al. 2017).  Ship survey data from 2009 resulted in an estimated total of 279,000 dolphins of the Delphinus delphis bairdii subspecies along the west coast of Baja California and the California coast (Carretta et al. 2011). A total of just over 12,000 Common Dolphins (Delphinus delphis delphis) was estimated in the EEZ of Colombia based on surveys conducted between 1986 and 2008 (Gerrodette and Palacios 1996).

Atlantic Ocean
The best estimate of abundance in the western North Atlantic is 172,825 (CV=0.21) based on Canadian and U.S. surveys conducted in 2016 (Hayes et al. 2020). Abundance in European continental shelf and offshore waters (not including the Mediterranean and Black seas) was estimated as 467,000 (CV=0.26) dolphins based on aerial and vessel surveys in 2016; the majority of sightings were in the Bay of Biscay and coastal waters of France and Spain (Hammond et al. 2017). Some 62,000 Common Dolphins were estimated to be present in 1993 west of the Bay of Biscay, in the area of the albacore tuna driftnet fishery (Goujon 1996).

Mediterranean Sea
Once one of the most common species in this region, Common Dolphins have experienced a generalized and major decline since the 1970s (Bearzi et al. 2003). In 2018, aerial surveys covering a large part of the region indicated low abundance across most of the Mediterranean subpopulation's range, and an absence or near absence of Common Dolphins within areas known to have hosted large numbers historically. The sum of mean estimates for the inner Mediterranean strata (Mediterranean minus the Alboràn Sea) was 5,200 Common Dolphins (95% CI 1890-14305; ASI 2020; Bearzi et al. 2020b). The Common Dolphin subpopulation in the Mediterranean region is listed as Endangered (Bearzi et al. 2020b).

Water bodies within the Mediterranean Sea
Common Dolphins have almost completely vanished from the Adriatic Sea, where they used to be abundant (Bearzi et al. 2004, Genov et al. 2020). In the Gulf of Vera, Balearic Sea, Common Dolphin numbers decreased threefold from 1992–1995 to 1996–2004 (Cañadas and Hammond 2008). Dramatic negative trends in abundance were recorded in the eastern Ionian Sea (Bearzi et al. 2006). Only a few individuals survive in the semi-enclosed Gulf of Corinth, Greece (Frantzis and Herzing 2002, Bearzi et al. 2016), where the subpopulation has been assessed as Critically Endangered (Santostasi et al. 2018, Bearzi et al. 2020a).

Black Sea
According to Birkun (2008), there may be at least several tens of thousands and possibly more than 100,000 Common Dolphins in the Black Sea. This population was, however, heavily hunted for centuries: over 160,000 animals were killed between 1962 and 1983, likely resulting in a significant population decline Birkun (2008). Aerial surveys carried out in 2019 in southern and western Black Sea waters resulted in 716 sightings of Common Dolphins involving 1751 individuals (Panigada et al. 2019). Abundance estimates from these surveys are not yet available.

Indian Ocean
No estimates exist for the northern Indian Ocean, and there are only a few for small areas of the southern Indian Ocean/Indo-Pacific. About 15,000–20,000 Common Dolphins were estimated to occur off South Africa (Cockcroft and Peddemors 1990), and approximately 21,000 were estimated for a localised region off southern Australia (Bilgmann et al. 2018).

Global totals
Taken together, the above estimates suggest a total of several million Common Dolphin worldwide. Considering that large portions of the species’ range have not been surveyed, especially in the Southern Hemisphere, the actual abundance is certainly higher than the sum of the estimates for the surveyed areas.
documentation.habitats:
Common Dolphins inhabit tropical and warm-temperate waters of the Pacific, Atlantic and Indian Oceans. In the Indo-Pacific, they are found mostly in continental shelf waters, and generally do not occur around oceanic islands far from mainland coasts (Jefferson and Van Waerebeek 2002). Elsewhere, Common Dolphins have been reported to prefer upwelling-modified waters, areas with steep sea-floor relief, and shelf areas (Evans 1994).

In the Mediterranean and in European waters generally, Common Dolphins inhabit both coastal (neritic) and offshore (pelagic) waters, but they seem to prefer continental shelf waters and areas of high productivity, such as upwelling regions (Bearzi et al. 2003, Saavedra et al. in press). In the Black Sea, Common Dolphins occur in both continental shelf and pelagic waters (Birkun 2008, Panigada et al. 2019).

The short-beaked form of common dolphins in the eastern central Pacific (Delphinus delphis delphis) extends far off the continental shelf in temperate waters with a distinct break in tropical equatorial waters.  The long-beaked form (Delphinus delphis bairdii)  in the same regions is strictly found in waters inshore of the shelf break (Hamilton et al. 2009). Associations with other marine mammal species are common. Mixed-species groups of Common and Striped Dolphins (Stenella coeruleoalba) are observed frequently in Mediterranean and European waters (Saavedra et al. In press). Common Dolphins also sometimes associate with Pilot Whales (Globicephala spp.) and a number of other small delphinids (Evans 1994, Quérouil et al. 2008).  Common Dolphins in the Eastern Tropical Pacific (ETP) are sometimes associated with Yellowfin Tuna (Thunnus albacares) and have thus been captured in tuna purse seines (Gerrodette 2018).

Common Dolphins are highly social animals that live in groups ranging from a few tens to several thousands of individuals (Perrin 2018, Saavedra et al. in press). Their prey normally consists of epipelagic and mesopelagic fishes and a smaller proportion of squids. Prey can include gadids, small scombroids, clupeoids and both loliginid and ommastrephid squids (Perrin 2018, Saavedra et al. in press). Diet studies suggest both opportunism and specialization (e.g. Santos et al. 2013), with a preference overall for energy-rich prey (Meynier et al. 2008, Spitz et al. 2010).
documentation.threats:
Common Dolphins are one of the most widespread, abundant and well-studied cetacean species.  As such there is a lot of information regarding threats, which is summarized below.  Despite this, much of the range includes remote, oceanic waters where threats are likely to be relatively low.

Bycatch
Globally, Common Dolphins are sometimes bycaught in fishing gear, including in purse seines, drifting and set gillnets, trawl nets, and longlines. In the Eastern Tropical Pacific, they are sometimes found in association with Yellowfin Tuna and the annual incidental mortality of Common Dolphins in the tuna purse-seine fishery was estimated to be as high as 24,000 in 1986 (IATTC 2017). After the Inter-American Tropical Tuna Commission (IATTC) imposed per-vessel catch limits on the international fleet, the mortality estimate of Common Dolphins declined to 127 in 2016 (IATTC 2017). Catches of Common Dolphins have also been recorded in purse-seine fisheries in the Indian Ocean and off the west coast of Africa (Anderson et al. 2020, Simmons 1968). Tuna driftnet fisheries in the Indian Ocean are estimated to have killed a total of 4.1 million small cetaceans between 1950-2018, an unknown proportion of which would have been Common Dolphins (Anderson et al. 2020). Common Dolphins were the most frequently reported cetaceans taken in the U.S. driftnet fishery for sharks and swordfish, with about 2,100 estimated killed between 1990 and 2002 (Julian and Beeson 1998, Carretta et al. 2005); measures taken since 1996 to reduce the cetacean bycatch in this fishery have been largely effective, and it is no longer a population-level concern for Common Dolphins (Carretta et al. 2006).

In the western Atlantic, average annual estimated fishery-related mortality of Common Dolphins during 2013–2017 was 419 individuals (CV=0.10), with the highest mortality occurring in the US mid-Atlantic bottom trawl fishery (Hayes et al. 2020). By-catches have also been reported from other areas and likely occur in most parts of the species’ range (Crespo et al. 2000, Bearzi et al. 2003, Saavedra et al. in press, Zerbini and Kotas 1998).

Incidental mortality in fishing gear, especially driftnets, has undoubtedly contributed to the decline of Common Dolphins in the Mediterranean (Bearzi et al. 2003). Driftnets were reported to kill a few hundred Common Dolphins per year in the Alboràn Sea alone during the early 1990s (Silvani et al. 1999). In EU waters, driftnets have been prohibited since 2002, but they are still being used illegally in much of the Mediterranean region.

Directed Takes
In the Black Sea large numbers of cetaceans were taken in directed hunts in the past. The total number of animals killed is not known, but it was estimated that before the mid 1950s Common Dolphins comprised 95% of the total number of Black Sea cetaceans killed in the former Soviet Union (Tzalkin 1940, Kleinenberg 1956). Based on this value, it was calculated that during the last five years of the cetacean hunt in the USSR and Bulgaria (1962–1966), these two countries landed over 121,000 Common Dolphins, while during the preceding 31 years (1931-61) another 1.5 million had been landed mainly by the USSR (Zemsky 1996). Between 1976 and 1981, D. d. ponticus was believed to account for 15–16% (or 37,500–40,000 individuals) of the Turkish catch, estimated for that period as 250,000 animals of all three species (IWC 1983, Birkun 2008). Directed takes of Common Dolphins for human consumption and shark bait are still a threat in Peru (Mintzer et al. 2018). In the 1990s many Common Dolphins were killed by harpooning around Margarita Island, off eastern Venezuela (Romero et al. 2001); it is not clear if such killing continues. The annual catch of Common Dolphins in the dolphin hunt in Japan in the early 1970s was over 8,000 individuals, peaking at 9,032 in 1973 (Kasuya 2017). The catch levels declined slowly, so that through most of the 1980s and early 1990s annual mortality was down to several hundred, and since 1993 it has been less than 10 animals (Kasuya 2017). Common Dolphins were (and may still be) taken in small numbers in the directed cetacean hunt in Sri Lanka (Ilangakoon et al. 1997).

Prey Depletion
Reduced prey availability resulting from overfishing was considered one of the primary causes of the regional decline of Common Dolphins in the Gulf of Vera, Spain (Cañadas and Hammond 2008), in the Gulf of Naples, Italy (Mussi et al. 2019), and in the Ionian Sea Archipelago, Greece (Bearzi et al. 2006, Piroddi et al. 2011). Of two mass mortality events that killed several hundred Black Sea Common Dolphins in 1990 and 1994 (Krivokhizhin and Birkun 1999), the latter was the result of a morbillivirus epizootic. However, both die-offs coincided with a drastic (8- to 12-fold) decline in the abundance of the two main Common Dolphin prey species, anchovy and sprat, and reduced prey availability is considered to be a major threat to Black Sea Common Dolphins (Bushuyev 2000). The correlation between large die-offs and prey scarcity suggests that the undernourishment has increased the dolphins’ susceptibility to viral infections in that area (Birkun 2008).

Other Threats
In European waters, Common Dolphins carry levels of PCBs that appear to be lower than those of other cetacean species (Jepson et al. 2016), but health issues likely due to PCBs are nonetheless observable. For instance, high concentrations of PCBs in Common Dolphins from the NE Atlantic were related to reproductive failure (Murphy et al. 2018).

Ingestion of plastic by marine organisms is a widespread and increasing problem, and possibly a significant cause of mortality among some cetaceans and may also threaten Common Dolphins (Simmonds 2012, Fossi et al. 2018). The stomachs of 35 Common Dolphins stranded in Galicia, NW Spain, all contained microplastics (Hernández-Gonzalez et al. 2018).

Noise produced by naval vessels and helicopters during a military exercise was considered the most probable cause of a mass stranding in the United Kingdom in 2008, involving at least 26 Common Dolphins (Jepson et al. 2013).
documentation.measures: Common Dolphins, along with other cetaceans, are legally protected in many countries although the extent of protection and degree of enforcement varies. The IATTC has imposed annual bycatch limits on each purse seiner and has promulgated regulations regarding the safe release of dolphins impacted by the ETP tuna purse seine fishery (Bayliff 2001). In the eastern North Pacific, the U.S. driftnet fishery has been required to use acoustic warning devices (pingers) since 1996 to reduce cetacean bycatch.
documentation.use_trade: This species was previously hunted in the Black Sea, but this hunt was closed in 1983 (Birkun 2008). Commercial hunting for human food has occurred for many years in Japan (Kasuya 2017) and this species is used as bait in some Indo-Pacific, South American, and Caribbean  fisheries (Romero et al. 1997, Van Waerebeek et al. 1997).
documentation.rationale:
In 2016 there was a change in taxonomy of the Delphinus genus and Delphinus capensis, formerly listed as Data Deficient on the Red List, is no longer recognised as a separate species. All Common Dolphins are now classified as Delphinus delphis and are covered in this updated Red List assessment.  

Common Dolphins are widely distributed from tropical to cool temperate waters of both hemispheres in all major ocean basins. They occur in a range of habitats from nearshore to offshore waters. They are one of the most widespread and abundant cetacean species globally. Available estimates indicate that there are well over 6 million individuals, and actual abundance is probably considerably higher, as many areas within the species range, especially in the Southern Hemisphere, have never been surveyed.

Common Dolphins are often bycaught in fishing gear throughout their range and several populations are of conservation concern, including the Black Sea subspecies, which is classified as Vulnerable (Birkun 2008), the Mediterranean subpopulation, which is Endangered (Bearzi 2003, Bearzi et al. 2020b), and the Gulf of Corinth subpopulation in Greece, which is Critically Endangered (Bearzi et al. 2020a). Other factors that likely affect the conservation status of Common Dolphins in some areas include prey depletion caused by overfishing, underwater noise, contamination by xenobiotics and global climate disruption. Despite this, the species remains one of the most widespread and abundant cetaceans and, although several local populations have declined dramatically, much of the range is in less impacted parts of the ocean, and there is no evidence that the threats are resulting in a global population decline. Delphinus delphis was listed (under the older taxonomic concept, excluding D. capensis) as Least Concern in 2008; it remains Least Concern in this updated assessment.
documentation.taxonomic_notes:
Until recently, two species were recognised in the genus Delphinus: the Short-beaked Common Dolphin (D. delphis) and the Long-beaked Common Dolphin (D. capensis), as described by Heyning and Perrin (1994). The morphological differences between D. delphis and D. capensis in the North Pacific (Heyning and Perrin 1994) were supported by molecular evidence from both mitochondrial and nuclear markers (Rosel et al. 1994). However, the genus exhibits a great deal of morphological variation globally and the criteria used to distinguish between the two species in the North Pacific appear not to apply elsewhere (Best 2007). In South Africa, Samaai et al. (2005) found that based on skull morphology the majority of specimens belonged to D. capensis, however two specimens were within the range for D. delphis from the North Pacific, and a third specimen fell between the ranges for D. delphis and D. capensis (Samaai et al. 2005). The same molecular markers that were used to differentiate the two sympatric species in the North Pacific failed to reveal any genetic distinction between the described morphotypes in South Africa (Best 2007).

Subsequently, Cunha et al. (2015), in a global analysis of Delphinus which included nine specimens from the west coast of South Africa (eastern South Atlantic), concluded that all specimens analysed from the Atlantic Ocean belonged to D. delphis, and that D. capensis was not a genetically valid species.

In 2016 the Society for Marine Mammalogy Committee on Taxonomy removed Delphinus capensis from its accepted list of marine mammal species and now recognises all Common Dolphins globally as belonging to a single species, Delphinus delphis (Committee on Taxonomy 2020). It recognises the following subspecies:

  • D. d. delphis Linnaeus, 1758. Common Dolphin
  • D. d. bairdii Dall, 1873. Eastern North Pacific Long-beaked Common Dolphin
  • D. d. ponticus Barabash, 1935. Black Sea Common Dolphin
  • D. d. tropicalis van Bree, 1971. Indo-Pacific Common Dolphin

Cunha et al. (2015) noted that because the sympatric or parapatric Long-beaked and Short-beaked Common Dolphins off California in the eastern North Pacific appear not to interbreed, the Long-beaked Common Dolphins might eventually be described and recognised as a separate species, D. bairdii. Some researchers have considered the Long-beaked Common Dolphins in the Indo-Pacific, which has an exceptionally long beak, to constitute a separate species, D. tropicalis (Van Bree and Gallagher 1978; Rice 1998). However, another morphometric study concluded that that form should be considered a subspecies (Jefferson and Van Waerebeek 2002) and it is currently recognised as such, D. delphis tropicalis.

The non-concordance of morphological and genetic data for Common Dolphins has caused much confusion and a rigorous global taxonomic study of the genus is needed. Further phylogenetic analyses are necessary to resolve the controversies surrounding the classification and nomenclature. More changes to Delphinus taxonomy should be expected.
